action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fazekas 1-2 white matter change, ventricles proportionate to sulci (Evans 0.30), normal midbrain, pons and putamina, and no basal ganglia, thalamic, nigral or mesial temporal signal change
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA, and here sequelae of the encephalitic illness [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproic acid level 72 mcg/mL (therapeutic) and ammonia 58 umol/L (mildly raised), liver tests normal
action_criteria.label: Valproate level and ammonia
action_criteria.rationale: Valproate can cause parkinsonism and hyperammonaemia even at therapeutic levels; the level and the ammonia tell how much it may contribute to the slowing

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Asymmetric reduction of dopamine transporter binding, worst in the right posterior putamen (SBR 0.94), with relative caudate sparing
action_criteria.label: DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) to separate a degenerative from a drug-related parkinsonism
action_criteria.rationale: Valproate and past olanzapine are live causes of parkinsonism here; pure drug-induced parkinsonism has normal presynaptic imaging, so an abnormal scan shows an underlying degenerative deficit [Marshall_2009]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: REM sleep without atonia in 48% of REM epochs with vigorous arm movements, vocalization and sitting up on video; AHI 3.2/h; PLMI 22/h
action_criteria.label: Video-polysomnography for the reported dream enactment
action_criteria.rationale: Two years of dream enactment with falls from bed have not been confirmed on PSG; REM sleep without atonia confirms RBD, a prodromal synucleinopathy marker that predates the encephalitic illness [Berg_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Slowed processing speed, executive and fluency deficits (TMT-A 48 s, TMT-B 118 s, FAS 28, animals 13) with preserved recall and naming
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery for the cognitive slowing
action_criteria.rationale: MoCA 24/30 with slowed responses, on valproate and with raised ammonia; a battery characterises the deficit and gives a baseline before treatment

action_criteria.expected_evidence: UPSIT 23/40, severe microsmia: olfactory loss on a validated test
action_criteria.label: Consider a validated smell identification test for the reported smell loss
action_criteria.rationale: Self-reported or bedside smell loss is not an MDS supportive criterion; olfactory loss on a validated test for age and sex is, and with no red flag it turns clinically probable into clinically established PD [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: The review names valproate-associated parkinsonism and raised ammonia with psychiatric planning of any switch, benzodiazepine fall risk, and alpha-blocker plus calcium-channel blocker hypotension with levodopa
action_criteria.label: Medication review before starting levodopa
action_criteria.rationale: Valproate may contribute to the parkinsonism and raises ammonia, clonazepam adds falls, and tamsulosin with amlodipine adds to levodopa's hypotensive effect

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not stop valproic acid abruptly or without psychiatric input in a patient with bipolar disorder
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in this older patient with cognitive slowing
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): bradykinesia with a left rest tremor and rigidity, no red flag, and no absolute exclusion (valproate is not a dopamine receptor blocker, and olanzapine was stopped about 20 months ago, before the motor onset); the abnormal DaTscan shows a presynaptic deficit that valproate does not cause, so valproate is at most a contributor; olfactory loss on a validated test (UPSIT 23/40, severe microsmia, when tested) is a second supportive criterion and makes it clinically established [Postuma_2015][Marshall_2009]

Plan any change of mood stabiliser with psychiatry: valproate can cause reversible parkinsonism and the ammonia is mildly raised (58 umol/L); lamotrigine has a lower tremor and parkinsonism burden; do not stop valproate abruptly

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months [NICE_NG71]
Make the bedroom safe for dream enactment, since he has fallen out of bed twice (bed rail or mattress on the floor, sharp objects removed)
If antipsychotic treatment is ever needed for his bipolar disorder or for psychosis, use quetiapine or clozapine

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

interactions: Valproate can cause reversible parkinsonism, and hyperammonaemia at therapeutic levels. Any change of mood stabiliser is planned with psychiatry. Lamotrigine has a lower tremor and parkinsonism burden.
Clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk with dopaminergic drugs in older patients.

Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) and amlodipine lower standing blood pressure and add to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
general.summary: No dopamine receptor blocker on the current list. Valproate: parkinsonism and hyperammonaemia. Clonazepam: sedation and falls. Tamsulosin and amlodipine with levodopa: additive hypotension.
warnings: Valproate: do not stop abruptly; withdrawal risks mood destabilisation.
Levodopa: nausea is common at initiation (take with food); postural hypotension and daytime sleepiness are possible.

metadata.difficulty_description: Multiple confounders complicate the diagnosis: a prior encephalitic illness suggesting post-encephalitic parkinsonism, chronic valproic acid use, which can cause reversible parkinsonism, past olanzapine, and a family history of essential tremor. The agent must see that the dream enactment and constipation predate the encephalitic illness and the parkinsonism began after olanzapine was stopped, and use the DaTscan to show a presynaptic deficit beyond valproate's effect.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Three drug and post-infectious explanations compete with PD; the DaTscan decides. Two required criteria (MRI and DaTscan).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Bernard Kaczmarek is a 68-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with a longstanding history of bipolar disorder type II who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of progressive motor slowing, stiffness, and a new tremor that have developed over the past 10 months. His wife, who accompanies him, first noticed that his facial expressions had become less animated and his voice softer approximately a year ago. Over the subsequent months she observed that he was walking more slowly with shorter steps and had begun to shuffle, particularly when turning. About 6 months ago he developed an intermittent tremor of his left hand that is most noticeable when the hand is at rest, such as when sitting watching television, and diminishes when he reaches for objects. He has also experienced progressive difficulty with fine motor tasks including buttoning his shirt, manipulating a fork, and his handwriting has become noticeably smaller. The patient attributes some of his symptoms to aging and residual effects from a significant illness 18 months ago. At that time he was hospitalized for approximately two weeks at an outside facility with high fevers, altered mental status, intermittent rigidity, and prolonged somnolence. He was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and eventually improved, though he and his wife feel he never fully returned to his prior baseline. The diagnosis at discharge was listed as encephalitis of uncertain etiology. His psychiatrist had discontinued olanzapine approximately 8 weeks before that hospitalization due to metabolic concerns, and his current psychiatric regimen of valproic acid and low-dose clonazepam has been stable for over a year. His wife also reports that for the past two years he has been increasingly active during sleep, talking loudly, flailing his arms, and on at least two occasions falling out of bed. His constipation has worsened progressively over the past three years despite daily polyethylene glycol. He denies visual hallucinations, urinary incontinence, or significant cognitive complaints, though his wife notes he is slower to respond in conversations and occasionally loses his train of thought. He denies any current use of antipsychotic medications or dopamine-blocking antiemetics.

neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (Myerson sign: fails to habituate). Mild seborrheic dermatitis on scalp and nasolabial folds. Reduced olfaction reported by patient but not formally tested. No myoclonus. No dystonia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing intact. Rapid alternating movements slowed bilaterally, left more than right, consistent with bradykinesia rather than cerebellar dysfunction.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal round and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact; no nystagmus. No oculogyric phenomena elicited during examination. Facial sensation intact to light touch and pinprick bilaterally. Marked facial hypomimia with reduced blink rate and decreased emotional expression. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Narrow-based gait with reduced stride length and decreased bilateral arm swing, left arm swing nearly absent. Mild forward-stooped posture. Mild festination noted on turns. Two to three corrective steps on pull test indicating mildly impaired postural reflexes. No freezing episodes observed. Able to rise from chair without arm assistance but slowly.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 24/30, losing points on trail-making (1), serial 7s (1), verbal fluency (1), abstraction (1), and delayed recall (2). Speech is hypophonic with mild monotone quality but content is fluent and coherent. No aphasia, neglect, or ideomotor apraxia. Affect somewhat flat but patient reports his mood is stable.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Moderate cogwheel rigidity at bilateral wrists, left greater than right. Mild axial rigidity noted on passive neck flexion. Bradykinesia evident on finger tapping, hand opening-closing, and pronation-supination, with progressive decrement in amplitude and speed, more prominent on the left. Mild resting tremor of the left hand at 4-5 Hz, suppressed with action. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at bilateral great toes. Vibration sense mildly reduced at bilateral ankles. Romberg test negative.
